<title>1TabPFN-2.5 performance on the standard TabArena-lite benchmark [], TabPFNv2 classification subset. TabPFN-2.5 outperforms any other model in a forward pass, and marks a strong leap from TabPFNv2. When fine-tuned on real data, Real-TabPFN-2.5 shows even stronger performance. The horizontal dotted line stands for AutoGluon 1.4 extreme mode tuned for 4 hours, an ensemble of models including TabPFNv2.</title>

<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<span id="p1.pic1.p2" class="ltx_para"><img src="2511.08667v1/figures/prior-logo.png" id="p1.pic1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:120/39;" width="120" height="39" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
<span id="p1.pic1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:173%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-2.5: Advancing the State of the Art in Tabular Foundation Models</span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Contributors" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Prior Labs Team</a><sup id="p1.pic1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:120%;">1</span></sup></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p2.3" class="ltx_p"><sup id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:80%;">1</span></sup><span id="p1.pic1.p2.3.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The list of contributors can be found in the <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Contributors" class="ltx_ref">appendix</a>.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="p1.pic1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The first tabular foundation model, TabPFN, and its successor TabPFNv2 have impacted tabular AI substantially, with dozens of methods building on it and hundreds of applications across different use cases. </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="p1.pic1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">This report introduces TabPFN-2.5, the next generation of our tabular foundation model, built for datasets with up to 50,000 data points and 2,000 features, a </span><math id="p1.pic1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="20\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">20</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" lspace="0.222em" mathcolor="#000000">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="p1.pic1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> increase in data cells compared to TabPFNv2. TabPFN-2.5 is now the leading method for the industry standard benchmark TabArena (which contains datasets with up to 100,000 training data points), substantially outperforming tuned tree-based models and matching the accuracy of AutoGluon 1.4, a complex four-hour tuned ensemble that even includes the previous TabPFNv2.
Remarkably, default TabPFN-2.5 has a 100% win rate against default XGBoost on small to medium-sized classification datasets (</span><math id="p1.pic1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">≤</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq</annotation></semantics></math><span id="p1.pic1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">10,000 data points, 500 features) and a 87% win rate on larger datasets up to 100K samples and 2K features (85% for regression).</span></span>
</span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<span id="p1.pic1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">For production use cases, we introduce a new distillation engine that converts TabPFN-2.5 into a compact MLP or tree ensemble, preserving most of its accuracy while delivering orders-of-magnitude lower latency and plug-and-play deployment.</span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p3.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">This new release will immediately strengthen the performance of the many applications and methods already built on the TabPFN ecosystem.</span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p3.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Date:<span id="p1.pic1.p3.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> November 6, 2025</span></span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p3.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p3.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Website:<span id="p1.pic1.p3.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <a href="https://priorlabs.ai/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://priorlabs.ai/</a></span></span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p3.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Docs:<span id="p1.pic1.p3.5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <a href="https://docs.priorlabs.ai/overview" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://docs.priorlabs.ai/overview</a></span></span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p3.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p3.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">PyPI:<span id="p1.pic1.p3.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <span id="p1.pic1.p3.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pip install tabpfn-client</span> (cloud SDK) or <span id="p1.pic1.p3.6.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pip install tabpfn</span> (local package)</span></span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p3.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p3.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">License:<span id="p1.pic1.p3.7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <span id="p1.pic1.p3.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TABPFN-2.5 License v1.0</span> (see Section <a href="#S6" title="6 License and Availability" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> for details)</span></span></span>

</span></span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.08667v1/tabarena-backup-hero-plot-10k-500.svg" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/176;" width="476" height="176"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">TabPFN-2.5 performance on the standard TabArena-lite benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, TabPFNv2 classification subset. TabPFN-2.5 outperforms any other model in a forward pass, and marks a strong leap from TabPFNv2. When fine-tuned on real data, Real-TabPFN-2.5 shows even stronger performance. The horizontal dotted line stands for AutoGluon 1.4 extreme mode tuned for 4 hours, an ensemble of models including TabPFNv2. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tabular data is ubiquitous, forming the backbone of decision-making in countless domains, from finance to healthcare. For decades, traditional tabular machine learning—built on gradient-boosted trees <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>, random forests <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, and linear or additive models—has been the workhorse of applied data science.
Yet these methods remain limited: they require extensive dataset-specific tuning, often provide uncalibrated or unreliable uncertainty estimates without significant modification, and lack the generalization and transferability of modern foundation models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Tabular foundation models (TFMs) offer a new paradigm. They address these limitations by pretraining on large synthetic distributions of tabular tasks and performing inference via in-context learning instead of gradient descent. They are training-free predictors meta-trained to yield strong calibration, without the need for time-consuming and labor-intensive hyperparameter tuning necessary for gradient-boosted trees. Their strong generalization makes them particularly attractive for data-scarce domains.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our initial release, TabPFNv1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> served as a proof-of-concept that a transformer could learn a Bayesian-like inference algorithm, though it was limited to small (up to 1k samples), clean, numerical-only data.
Our successor, TabPFNv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, scaled this idea into a practical model for datasets up to 10,000 samples. TabPFNv2 handles the messy and heterogeneous data seen in the real world—including categorical features, missing values, and outliers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This paper describes the next release of TabPFN: TabPFN-2.5.
Our key contributions are:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SOTA Performance:</span> In a forward pass, TabPFN-2.5 outperforms tuned tree-based models (like XGBoost and CatBoost) and matches the accuracy of AutoGluon 1.4 tuned for 4 hours—a complex ensemble that includes all previous methods, even TabPFNv2.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Improved Scalability:</span> We scale the power of in-context learning to datasets of up to 50,000 samples (5x increase over TabPFNv2) and 2,000 features (4x increase), making TFMs viable for a much wider range of real-world problems <span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                  <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                  
                  
                  
                In exploratory runs, classification datasets up to <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>160k rows <math id="footnote1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 500 features and regression datasets up to <math id="footnote1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>85k <math id="footnote1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 500 features fit into memory on an NVIDIA H100 (80 GB) using FP16 and FlashAttention-3. These configurations are outside our validated range and not included in reported benchmarks.</span></span></span>. While TabPFN-2.5 was designed for up to 50,000 rows, we note that this limit is not strict and report strong results on benchmarks with up to 100,000 training samples.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fast Inference:</span> We dramatically improve inference speed. We introduce TabPFN-as-MLP/TreeEns, a proprietary output engine, that yields an MLP or tree ensemble, combining most of TabPFN’s
accuracy with the low-latency inference and easy deployment of MLPs and tree ensembles.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We begin by surveying the growing ecosystem of TabPFN applications and extensions (Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Ecosystem &amp; Adoption" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). We then describe our methodological advances (Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Model Overview" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) and present the experimental results (Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). We then discuss how to get the best speed out of TabPFN on common hardware (Section <a href="#S5" title="5 How to Get Optimal Fit + Predict Speed from TabPFN-2.5" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) as well as our non-commercial open-source license (Section <a href="#S6" title="6 License and Availability" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).
We conclude by discussing the remaining limitations and opportunities for future work (Sections <a href="#S7" title="7 Conclusion and The Road Ahead" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). For installation and usage examples, see the online documentation at
<a href="https://docs.priorlabs.ai/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://docs.priorlabs.ai/</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Ecosystem &amp; Adoption</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now discuss community adoption, methods built on top of TabPFN, and our TabPFN extensions.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Community Adoption</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since its release, TabPFNv2 has become a widely used baseline for tabular ML. The <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Nature</span> paper <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> has been cited in almost 400 papers within 10 months of its publication, and the open-source package has surpassed 2,000,000 downloads on PyPI<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            Google Scholar entry (accessed Nov 6, 2025; Download stats for <span id="footnote2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">tabpfn</span> on pepy.tech (accessed Nov 6, 2025): <a href="https://www.pepy.tech/project/tabpfn" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.pepy.tech/project/tabpfn</a></span></span></span>. Adoption spans both research and production, especially in settings with sparse data or frequent retraining requirements. This widespread adoption has matured TabPFN from a research model into a stable product. With feedback from our community of nearly 1,500 users on Discord, and hundreds of closed GitHub issues, we have shipped numerous stability fixes, and cross-platform device compatibility. In addition to commercial use-cases, we also collected 100 published use cases across a broad range of areas (please see Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B TabPFN Use Case Overview" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for a detailed list):</p>
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Healthcare and Life Sciences.</span> Adoption is strongest in healthcare (50+ published applications), driven by TabPFN’s exceptional performance in data-scarce settings—a common challenge in medicine. Use cases span oncology, neurology, cardiology, and pharmacology, powering applications like diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment response prediction from complex multimodal (clinical, imaging, omics) data.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Financial Services, Banking, and Insurance.</span> While we see strong commercial traction, public-facing use cases are rare due to the competitive, private nature of this industry (3 collected). Applications in this domain typically involve proprietary forecasting, uplift modeling, and risk assessments.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Energy and Utilities.</span> We’ve identified 15 published cases centered on complex forecasting and optimization. Key applications include environmental forecasting (algal blooms, wildfire risk), renewable-energy nowcasting, and process/asset optimization across water, oil &amp; gas.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Manufacturing and Industrial.</span> The 12 diverse published use cases in this area highlight TabPFN’s flexibility. Applications include anomaly detection in IIoT security, predictive maintenance for rotating machinery, physics-aware optimization for battery thermal modeling, and semiconductor test optimization.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Other Industries</span> 19 further applications demonstrate broad utility, spanning geoscience, agriculture, materials, and engineering. These range from microbiome classification and lunar regolith analysis to soil property modeling, fuel-blend optimization and crop yield forecasting.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>A Foundational Layer for New Research</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond direct application, TabPFN now serves as a foundational layer for new research domains. Its ability to act as a powerful, pre-trained “algorithm-in-a-box” has unlocked new approaches to complex problems. We expect TabPFN-2.5 to directly boost performance in all these areas:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S2.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Time Series Forecasting</span>: TabPFN-TS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> extends TabPFN to time-series forecasting by incorporating temporal context into its in-context learning mechanism, outperforming specialized time-series models without any retraining.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Node Classification in Graphs:</span> Various works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> represent graph nodes as tabular instances with relational and structural features, directly using tabular foundation models like TabPFN to solve the problem.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Data Streams:</span>
TabPFNv2 was used for in-context learning on Evolving Data Streams <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>. TabPFN can <em id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">adapt to non-stationary data streams</em> online, without retraining, enabling continual learning in evolving environments.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reinforcement Learning:</span>
TabPFNv2 was used to replace gradient-based policy optimization with in-context optimization over trajectories, creating a powerful general-purpose optimizer for RL tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bayesian optimization: </span>
GIT-BO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> uses TabPFNv2 inside of high-dimensional Bayesian Optimization, as it enables efficient search in high-dimensional and heterogeneous design spaces.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multimodal Learning &amp; Encoding:</span> TabPFN is used to integrate tabular data with other modalities. It can serve as a <em id="S2.I2.i6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">frozen tabular encoder</em> to generate robust embeddings for combination with data like images (e.g., in the TIME framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>), or handle modalities in a unified manner by adding modality-specific projectors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i7" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Causal Inference:</span> Do-PFN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, CausalPFN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, and CausalFM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> pre-train PFNs to predict interventional outcomes, and show strong performance in estimating causal effects.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>The TabPFN-Extensions Ecosystem</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We maintain the TabPFN–Extensions repository (<a href="https://github.com/PriorLabs/tabpfn-extensions" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/PriorLabs/tabpfn-extensions</a>), which offers extensions around the core model, developed together with a growing community around TabPFN. These extensions leverage TabPFN capabilities for:</p>
<ul id="S2.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Interpretability.</span> SHAP values, feature selection, partial dependence.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Unsupervised Tasks.</span> Data generation, augmentation, outlier detection.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I3.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Advanced Modeling.</span> Many-class classification, regression-via-classifier.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I3.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I3.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Performance &amp; Integration.</span> Lightweight HPO, ensembling, and integration with tree/forest baselines.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A5.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ Appendix E The TabPFN Ecosystem" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> in the appendix provides a minimal workflow to help users pick the right components for their task.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Model Overview</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN-2.5 follows the same general design as TabPFNv2 but introduces deeper architectures, richer synthetic priors, and new calibration and inference modules. We summarize only the key changes here.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We improved our prior data generation substantially, broadened the set of distributions and scaled up to more data points and more features, while keeping the prediction tasks difficult. Like the original TabPFNv2, TabPFN-2.5 is trained purely on synthetically generated data.
We also release a version that is fine-tuned on real data following Real-TabPFN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>. It is trained on a curated corpus of <span id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> 43 real-world tabular datasets</span> sourced from OpenML and Kaggle, deduplicated against all internal benchmarks and the full TabArena suite. We refer to this version as Real-TabPFN-2.5, and report strong improvement in Figures <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ A significant improvement upon TabPFNv2. ‣ 4.1 Performance on the Industry Standard Benchmark TabArena ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ A significant improvement upon TabPFNv2. ‣ 4.1 Performance on the Industry Standard Benchmark TabArena ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. See Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Data Contamination and Deduplication for Real-TabPFN-2.5" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> for details on training and deduplication.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Architecture.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow the alternating-attention transformer design of TabPFNv2, which attends across both data points and features to achieve permutation invariance, but introduces some changes:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We increase the network depth from 12 to 18 layers for our regression model and 24 layers for our classification model.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We simultaneously increase the feature group size (the number of features being embedded together), which allows for faster training and inference. We use a group size of 3 for TabPFN-2.5, compared to 2 for TabPFNv2.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For our regression models, we found a small improvement by replacing the linear encoder used in TabPFNv2 by a 2-layer MLP.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we add 64 additional “thinking” rows to the input dataset of TabPFN-2.5, which are learned during pretraining. Inspired by results from the LLM literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, these rows give additional computational capacity to the model and can also act as attention sinks to help the model ignore other rows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Other core components from TabPFNv2—feature/sample dual attention, caching separation of training/test context, and positional feature embeddings—remain unchanged.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Preprocessing.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We aggregate predictions across multiple dataset permutations and feature transformations to enhance robustness and generalization.
In the updated TabPFN-2.5 configuration, additional feature transformations are introduced to enhance robustness against outlier-prone feature distributions and to increase the diversity among the individual estimators. Specifically, we combine robust scaling and soft clipping (following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>) with quantile transformations and standard scaling to balance stability and sensitivity across features. Following TabPFNv2, we also include singular value decomposition (SVD) components as additional features in some of the estimators, capturing high-energy directions of variance that provide complementary global structure information.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hyperparameter Tuning of TabPFN with TabPFN.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN’s hyperparameter space spans architectural, training, and prior-data parameters, making exhaustive grid search computationally infeasible. To explore this space efficiently, we adopted a surrogate-based optimization strategy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We first trained <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 100</annotation></semantics></math> models on a broad but sparse grid of hyperparameter configurations drawn from plausible prior ranges and evaluated them on a curated in-house validation suite, producing a compact set of hyperparameter–performance pairs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">With <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 50</annotation></semantics></math> hyperparameters and only <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> datapoints, direct interpolation was prone to overfitting. We therefore used a regression model well-suited for data-scarce structured prediction—our previous TabPFNv2 model—as a surrogate to predict validation performance over a denser grid of <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> configurations. This self-referential “TabPFN-tunes-TabPFN” strategy efficiently surfaced promising regions of the search space for full, compute-intensive training runs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tuning custom metrics.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN-2.5 adds new post-processing capabilities that enhance both calibration and metric-specific optimization. Our framework now supports tuning the classifier’s decision threshold, enabling direct optimization of metrics beyond accuracy—such as the F1-score—by adjusting the operating point to the desired trade-off between precision and recall. For multiclass classification, it allows to apply temperature scaling to the final softmax outputs to improve probability calibration. This threshold tuning procedure can yield substantial performance improvements (see Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Results with Tuned Decision Thresholds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>). Unless otherwise noted, however, all classification results in this report are computed using uncalibrated, default scores, without temperature scaling or threshold tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reducing inference costs.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite being a larger model than TabPFNv2, TabPFN-2.5 is between 1x and 2.3x faster thanks to optimized preprocessing and larger feature groups, as shown in Figure <a href="#A9.F20" title="Figure 20 ‣ Appendix I Supplementary Inference Time Details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a>. This allows TabPFN-2.5 to scales inference to datasets with up to <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> rows and 2,000 features. Furthermore, we found large speed gain in this adoption of FlashAttention-3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> and parallel evaluation across multiple GPUs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Creating fast, deployable models.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To improve deployment flexibility, we developed a proprietary distillation engine that, given a training data set, outputs a multi-layer perceptron (TabPFN-2.5-as-MLP) or tree ensemble classifier (TabPFN-2.5-as-TreeEns) whose performance is close to the one of TabPFN on this dataset (see Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ TabPFN-2.5 shows strong results up to 50,000 samples and 2,000 features. ‣ 4.2 Performance on Internal Benchmarks ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).
In contrast to TabPFN, this resulting MLP or tree ensemble classifier is dataset-specific, does not perform in-context learning, takes as input a single data point, and has very low latency and memory footprint for making predictions. It can also be seamlessly integrated into existing production pipelines, including those constrained by latency, interpretability, or regulatory requirements that hinder a change in the class of models being deployed.
This increases TabPFN-2.5’s practical use in real-world decision systems. Other types of models could easily be supported.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.fig3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experimental Results</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the industry standard benchmark TabArena and using our own benchmarking framework. Then, we report our advances to reduce inference latency. Finally, we demonstrate that TabPFN-2.5 yields new state-of-the-art performance for causal machine learning.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Performance on the Industry Standard Benchmark TabArena</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TabArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> is the most curated tabular benchmark, based on the largest number of candidate datasets considered, and created by open-source contributors from a wide range of institutions. It will appear at the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets &amp; Benchmarks track and is thus most up-to-date. We follow the paper’s recommendation to benchmark on “TabArena-Lite”, which is a cheaper but representative version of the full benchmark using only one test fold. The benchmark contains a set of 51 datasets selected from 1053 to be representative of real-world tabular data. See <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Erickson et al. [1]</a></cite> for the list of datasets.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pushing the limit on small to medium-sized datasets.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ A significant improvement upon TabPFNv2. ‣ 4.1 Performance on the Industry Standard Benchmark TabArena ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows results for TabPFN-2.5 on TabArena-Lite with up to 10,000 data points and 500 features, demonstrating that TabPFN-2.5, in a forward pass, outperforms the wide range of existing tabular prediction methods. On classification, TabPFN-2.5 in a forward pass outperforms AutoGluon 1.4, an ensemble tuned for four hours and including best other methods (even TabPFNv2). Using our Real-TabPFN-2.5 variant fine-tuned on real datasets (deduplicated from TabArena datasets) widens the lead even further. On the other hand, our regression model benefits much more from tuning and outperforms AutoGluon 1.4 after being tuned for 60 configurations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scaling to larger datasets.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ A significant improvement upon TabPFNv2. ‣ 4.1 Performance on the Industry Standard Benchmark TabArena ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows a similar experiment on all the TabArena datasets, with up to 100,000 data points and 2,000 features, clearly ranking TabPFN-2.5 as the best default model, and outperforming (for regression datasets) or approaching (for classification datasets) AutoGluon 1.4 (tuned for 4 hours) when tuned. Again, we highlight the very strong default performance of Real-TabPFN-2.5 on these larger classification datasets, beating in one forward pass any other tuned and ensembled model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">A significant improvement upon TabPFNv2.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Comparing the default performance of TabPFN-2.5 and TabPFNv2, we see a big leap in performance in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ A significant improvement upon TabPFNv2. ‣ 4.1 Performance on the Industry Standard Benchmark TabArena ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. In addition, looking at performance on each dataset in TabArena (TabPFNv2 compatible subset) in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Creating fast, deployable models. ‣ 3 Model Overview" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we see that TabPFN-2.5 clearly outperforms TabPFNv2 on almost all datasets, and is never much worse. In Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Detailed TabArena Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>, we detail the results on TabArena-Lite, showing the pairwise win rates of the different models, and comparing TabPFN-2.5 to other foundation models like TabICL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> or LimiX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<div id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_block ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:165.6pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.08667v1/tuning-impact-elo-horizontal_results_with_9vwfdmbi_with_tabpfnv2_new_classification_0-10k_below_500_features.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:303/260;" width="303" height="260"></object>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Performance on Internal Benchmarks</h3>

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">A diverse internal benchmark.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the public TabArena benchmark, we built our own benchmarking framework using proprietary data. It includes over 100 use cases from healthcare, finance, insurance, retail and manufacturing. This benchmark focuses on comparing to gradient-boosted decision tree libraries that are frequently used in industry (XGBoost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, CatBoost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, LightGBM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>), both in their default version and tuned for one hour.
In all cases, we show the results of three standard gradient-boosted tree libraries (LightGBM, XGBoost and CatBoost). We tune all of the baselines for 1hr, using random search on the established search spaces from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. TabPFN is tuned using our AutoTabPFN system, resulting in a tuned and ensembled model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">TabPFN-2.5 shows strong results up to 50,000 samples and 2,000 features.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ TabPFN-2.5 shows strong results up to 50,000 samples and 2,000 features. ‣ 4.2 Performance on Internal Benchmarks ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ TabPFN-2.5 shows strong results up to 50,000 samples and 2,000 features. ‣ 4.2 Performance on Internal Benchmarks ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> show results on our internal benchmark for classification and regression datasets with up to 50,000 data points and 500 features. We can see on these figures that TabPFN outperforms in one forward pass all our tuned baselines. In Section <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Additional Internal Benchmark Details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>, we also show strong results on datasets with 500 to 2,000 features, and provide more details on how we normalize the performance of each model across datasets.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4">
<figure id="S4.F5.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.08667v1/barplot_stacked_multiclass_full_methods_narrower_acc.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/568;" width="476" height="568"></object>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4">
<figure id="S4.F5.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.08667v1/barplot_stacked_multiclass_full_methods_narrower_roc.svg" id="S4.F5.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/568;" width="476" height="568"></object>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4">

<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Measuring TabPFN-2.5 Training and Inference Speed</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.3 Measuring TabPFN-2.5 Training and Inference Speed ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> shows how TabPFN-2.5 classification speed scales with training set size, when using one or four GPUs, as we vary the number of rows and columns in the dataset. The time measured includes both the time to process the training rows (equivalent to the combination of “training” a classical ML model) and “prediction” time on test rows.
We can observe the expected scaling in <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(r^{2}\min(c,500)+r\min(c,500)^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>500</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>500</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(r^{2}\min(c,500)+r\min(c,500)^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of rows and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of columns, due to dual attention over rows and capped per-estimator feature subsampling at 500 features.
Section <a href="#S5" title="5 How to Get Optimal Fit + Predict Speed from TabPFN-2.5" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> contains results for regression, performance on common models of GPU, for reference, and a measurement of the speedup from TabPFNv2. The inference speed reported here reflects the latency of the full in-context learning model.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F8" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F8.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2511.08667v1/latency_heatmap_h100_x1_multiclass.png" id="S4.F8.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="width:19.459em; height:11.057em;aspect-ratio:324/184;" width="324" height="184" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F8.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S4.F8.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">one H100 GPU</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F8.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2511.08667v1/latency_heatmap_h100_x4_multiclass.png" id="S4.F8.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="width:19.390em; height:11.057em;aspect-ratio:322/184;" width="322" height="184" alt="Refer to caption">

Time taken, in seconds, to fit TabPFN-2.5 classification models on various training set sizes, and then make predictions on <math id="S4.F8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="500" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>500</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">500</annotation></semantics></math> test rows.
Figure <a href="#A9.F18" title="Figure 18 ‣ Appendix I Supplementary Inference Time Details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a> in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 How to Get Optimal Fit + Predict Speed from TabPFN-2.5" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> reports results for regression, alongside performance on A100 and T4 GPUs.
</span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Fast Inference with TabPFN-2.5-as-MLP</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We benchmark TabPFN-2.5-as-MLP against tuned LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost models, as well as the standard TabPFN-2.5 model, on our curated collection of internal open source datasets with less than 10k data points. Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ TabPFN-2.5 shows strong results up to 50,000 samples and 2,000 features. ‣ 4.2 Performance on Internal Benchmarks ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> illustrates representative test-split performance. Empirically, TabPFN-2.5-as-MLP offers competitive accuracy while reducing inference cost, making it attractive for high-throughput or resource-constrained deployment scenarios.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>TabPFN for Causal Inference</h3>

<section id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">RealCause Benchmark.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To systematically evaluate TabPFN’s potential as a causal estimator, we leverage the RealCause benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, a semi-synthetic benchmark which begins with real-world randomized control trial (RCT) data and synthetically creates observable confounding effects.<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
                
                
                
              Descriptions of the ACIC-2016, IHDP, and Lalonde-PSID and Lalonde-CPS datasets are provided in Appendix Table <a href="#A4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Importance of Base Model. ‣ Appendix D Details on Causal Inference Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</span></span></span> We measure the Precision in Estimating Heterogeneous Effects (PEHE), which corresponds to the root-mean-squared error between predicted and RealCause’s ground-truth CATE values<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
                
                
                
              For a description of the CATE estimation task and common estimators, please refer to Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Details on Causal Inference Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</span></span></span>. In Figure <a href="#S4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Foundation Models for Causal Inference. ‣ 4.5 TabPFN for Causal Inference ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, we show that PFN-based methods for CATE-estimation dominate the leaderboard, occupying the first seven positions. TabPFN-2.5 applied as a T-Learner, a simple two-model approach that fits a separate model to the treatment and control observations, achieves the strongest overall performance, outperforming specialized tree- and deep-learning-based methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>. We also observe in Figure <a href="#S4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Foundation Models for Causal Inference. ‣ 4.5 TabPFN for Causal Inference ‣ 4 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> that for each of our three meta-learners, TabPFN-2.5 performs better out-of-the-box than TabPFNv2 and HPO<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
                
                
                
              Hyperparameter optimization is run for 60 seconds on an H100 per propensity and outcome model using FLAML <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>.</span></span></span>. This result shows that improvements in base model predictive performance transfer to the problem of causal inference.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Foundation Models for Causal Inference.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While we show strong results in unconfounded settings, real-world causal inference often involves imperfect data and latent confounders. A growing line of work aims to pre-train PFNs explicitly for causal reasoning—for example, predicting interventional outcomes or learning causal structures directly <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>. We view this as one of the most exciting frontiers for foundation models: extending TabPFN’s reasoning from predicting <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">what is</span> to inferring <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">what would happen if</span>, and ultimately, <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">understanding why</span>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F10" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F10.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:165.6pt;"><img src="2511.08667v1/figures/realcause_pretty.png" id="S4.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:677/677;" width="677" height="677" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F10.fig1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="S4.F10.fig1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
PFN-based CATE estimators dominate RealCause, outperforming specialized tree- and deep-learning-based methods for causal inference. Choice of propensity and outcome model is important for CATE estimation.
</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F10.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:165.6pt;"><img src="2511.08667v1/figures/realcause_pretty_tabpfn.png" id="S4.F10.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:1354/1352;" width="1354" height="1352" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F10.fig2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 10</span>: </span><span id="S4.F10.fig2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Improvements in base model predictive performance transfer to improved performance in CATE estimation. Our new model, TabPFN-2.5, is the strongest choice of base model for all meta-learners.
</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>How to Get Optimal Fit + Predict Speed from TabPFN-2.5</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To achieve good performance, we recommend the following:</p>
<ul id="S5.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Use a dedicated GPU or GPUs</span>: We recommend NVIDIA H100 or A100 GPUs. Any dedicated GPU supported by PyTorch is compatible, but some models may not have enough memory for larger datasets or perform slowly.
Integrated GPUs, MPS (Apple Silicon), and CPUs are also supported, but are only suitable for small datasets.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Use multiple GPUs</span>: For larger datasets, fit + predict time can be dramatically reduced by parallelizing inference over several GPUs. To enable this, set the <span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">device</span> parameter of <span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TabPFNClassifier</span> and <span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TabPFNRegressor</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Use batch inference</span>: Unless the fitted-model cache is enabled (see below), the model is retrained each time <span id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">.predict()</span> is called. This means that it is much faster to make a prediction for all your test points in a single <span id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">.predict()</span> call. If you run out of memory, split the test points into batches of <math id="S5.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1000</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10000</annotation></semantics></math> and call <span id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">.predict()</span> for each batch.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Use PyTorch 2.8 or above</span>: TabPFN-2.5 also supports earlier versions of PyTorch, but these may have lower performance.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">For small datasets, enable the fitted-model cache</span>:
This is an experimental feature that trains and stores the model during <span id="S5.I1.i5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">.fit()</span>, making subsequent <span id="S5.I1.i5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">.predict()</span> calls fast by using a KV-Cache. It is enabled by setting the <span id="S5.I1.i5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">fit_mode</span> parameter of <span id="S5.I1.i5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TabPFNClassifier</span> and <span id="S5.I1.i5.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TabPFNRegressor</span> to <span id="S5.I1.i5.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">fit_with_cache</span>.
However, with this setting classification models will consume approximately 6.1 KB of GPU memory and 48.8 KB of CPU memory per cell in the training dataset (regression models about <math id="S5.I1.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>25</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25</annotation></semantics></math>% less), thus it is currently only suitable for small training datasets. For larger datasets and CPU-based inference, we recommend the TabPFN-as-MLP/Tree output engine.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If speed is important for your application, you may consider optimizing the <span id="S5.I1.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">memory_saving_mode</span> and <span id="S5.I1.i6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n_preprocessing_jobs</span> parameters of <span id="S5.I1.i6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TabPFNClassifier</span> and <span id="S5.I1.i6.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TabPFNRegressor</span>. See the code documentation for further information.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A9.F18" title="Figure 18 ‣ Appendix I Supplementary Inference Time Details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a> in the appendix shows the inference latency you can expect for three common models of GPU, when using one or four GPUs.
It also shows the maximum dataset size that fits in memory for each GPU.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>License and Availability</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We release TabPFN-2.5 under our <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TABPFN-2.5 License v1.0</span> designed to be permissive for research and internal evaluation. It <span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">explicitly allows</span> testing, evaluation, and internal benchmarking, so an organization can download the model and run preliminary assessments on its own datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The key restriction is that the model, its derivatives, and its outputs cannot be used for any commercial or production purpose. This includes, but is not limited to, revenue-generating products, competitive benchmarking for procurement, client deliverables, or using the model’s results for internal commercial decision-making.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For production use cases, we offer a <span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Commercial Enterprise License</span>. This provides access to our proprietary high-speed inference engine, dedicated support, integration tooling, and other internal models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Please contact us at sales@priorlabs.ai for commercial licensing inquiries. The full non-commercial mode license text can be found at <a href="https://huggingface.co/Prior-Labs/tabpfn_2_5/blob/main/LICENSE" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/Prior-Labs/tabpfn_2_5/blob/main/LICENSE</a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Cloud API</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide a managed TabPFN-2.5 cloud endpoint, which runs on our optimized GPU infrastructure. This is the recommended option for users who do not have a dedicated local GPU or for those who wish to use TabPFN commercially without purchasing a full on-premise license.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The API is accessible via a simple Python SDK<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
              
              
              
            The Python client SDK is available on PyPI: <a href="https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN-client" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN-client</a></span></span></span> (<span id="S6.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pip install tabpfn-client</span>) or a standard REST API, allowing for integration into both non-commercial and commercial applications.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion
and The Road Ahead</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We are excited about this release.
Taken together, our experiments on public (TabArena) and private benchmarks demonstrate that TabPFN-2.5 sets a new state-of-the-art for tuning-free tabular models. Built for datasets up to 50,000 rows and 2,000 features, TabPFN-2.5 matches the performance of complex 4-hour-tuned ensembles - ensembles that even include our previous TabPFNv2 - and in a forward pass outperforms any other tuned model on the unrestricted public TabArena benchmark (which contains datasets with up to 100,000 training data points).</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The next step is scaling to datasets with millions of rows. We are actively developing new techniques - including retrieval, fine-tuning, and novel architectures - and anticipate that systems based on Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) will define state-of-the-art performance for datasets with millions of data points very soon.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our broader vision beyond this release is to tackle the entire stack of problems with tabular-like data, including time series, multimodal tabular data, causal inference, unsupervised tasks, integration of domain knowledge and decision support, ultimately building the core intelligence engine for reasoning over structured and multimodal data.</p>
</div>
</section>
